<details><summary>Key for A16.10 (open only after your attempt)</summary>

- **Q1:** B. A week has 604800 seconds and 0.0001 of it is 60.48 seconds; the primer's table says 1 minute 5 seconds, which is wrong.
- **Q2:** A, B, C. D is false: every extra nine divides the budget by ten.
- **Q3:** 302.4 seconds (tolerance ±0.1). A week has 604800 seconds and 0.05 percent of that is 302.4 seconds.
- **Q4 (marking outline):** A read is stale if at least one write arrived in the last 0.2 s. For Poisson arrivals with rate 0.5 the number of writes in 0.2 s has probability e to the power of minus 0.1 of being zero. So the stale fraction is 1 minus e to the minus 0.1, which is about 0.095, that is 9.5 percent.
- **Q5 (what a passing submission shows):** The four-nines week is 60.5 seconds, five components of 99.9 percent in series give 99.50 percent, three in parallel give 99.9999999 percent, and the simulated stale fraction is within 0.5 points of 9.5 percent.

</details>

### U16.11 Scaling the data tier: replication, federation, sharding, denormalization, SQL tuning, and choosing between SQL and NoSQL
**Sources:** SDP RDB, NOSQL, SQLNO
- **Topics:** the relational database management system (RDBMS) as a collection of tables with the ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability; the theory is in U15.20) and the six techniques the primer lists to scale it: master-slave replication (the master serves reads and writes and replicates to slaves that serve reads, in a tree if needed; if the master fails the system runs read-only until a slave is promoted); master-master replication (both serve reads and writes and coordinate on writes; a load balancer or application logic decides where to write; loose consistency or higher write latency; conflict resolution) and the disadvantages of replication (possible data loss, replicas bogged down replaying writes, replication lag growing with more slaves, single-threaded replay, extra hardware); federation or functional partitioning (separate forums, users and products databases, less traffic and lag each, but joins across databases are harder and the application must know where to go); sharding (distribute data across databases so each holds a subset, such as users by last-name initial or by geography; less traffic, replication and index size and more cache hits; the disadvantages are application complexity, lopsided data from power users, rebalancing, hard joins; consistent hashing reduces the data moved); denormalization (redundant copies to avoid expensive joins, for example materialized views, since reads can outnumber writes 100:1 or 1000:1; the disadvantages are duplicated data and heavy-write cost); SQL tuning (benchmark with a load tool and profile with the slow query log; tighten the schema: CHAR for fixed length, TEXT for large text, INT up to 2^32, DECIMAL for currency, no large BLOBs, VARCHAR(255) and the 8-bit length, NOT NULL; use good indices (B-trees, extra space and slower writes, disabling indices during a bulk load); avoid expensive joins; partition tables; tune the query cache). NoSQL as key-value store (abstraction: hash table), document store (key-value store with documents as values, for example MongoDB, CouchDB and DynamoDB), wide column store (nested map of column families, row key and timestamp; Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra) and graph database (abstraction: graph); BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency); SQL or NoSQL: the primer's reasons for SQL (structured data, strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions, clear patterns for scaling, established tools, fast index lookups) and for NoSQL (semi-structured data, dynamic or flexible schema, non-relational data, no complex joins, many TB or PB of data, data-intensive workload, very high IOPS throughput) and the sample data well-suited for NoSQL (clickstream and log ingest, leaderboard or scoring data, temporary data such as a shopping cart, hot tables, metadata and lookup tables).
- **Results:** a single-threaded replica applying writes behaves as a queue, so its mean time in the system is 1/(μ − λ): at 90% write load it is 10 service times and at 30% it is 1.43, 7 times less, and the waiting time in the queue falls 21 times, which is why federation, by splitting the write load three ways, cuts lag far more than 3 times [D, check]; with a hash by user over 16 shards under a Zipf load the hottest shard carries 2.06 times the mean (4 shards: 1.22), and one user alone is 8.3% of the load against a fair shard share of 6.25%, so hashing cannot fix a single hot key [D, check]; adding an 11th node moves about 8.3% of the keys under consistent hashing (ideal 1/11 = 9.1%) but 91.1% under hash mod N, and 100 virtual nodes per server bring the load maximum from 2.24 to 1.20 times the mean [D, check]; INT holds 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 values, so 360 million shortlinks fit with a margin of about 12 times [D, check]; denormalizing d copies trades one join of j lookups per read for d writes per update, so it wins when reads per write exceed d/j, and the primer's 100:1 ratio makes d = 5 copies cheap [D]; the choice SQL or NoSQL is made from the access pattern and consistency need, not from fashion (the polyglot answer is both, U10.6) [S].
- **Build:** a replica-lag simulation (U15.22's schedulers are not needed), the consistent-hash ring of U9.5 (the owner) driven by a skewed-load shard simulator, and a small denormalization experiment in `sqlite3` comparing a three-table join with a materialized summary table under a 100:1 read mix; the cloud routes are the managed relational and NoSQL services of U10.7. [local]
- **Go track:** the sharding exercise is written in Go (enter U23.6): the consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes (maximum-to-mean load 2.22, 1.58, 1.16 and 1.04 for 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 virtual nodes, and 9.46% of keys moved when a node joins). [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kleppmann chapters 5 and 6 on replication and partitioning; Karger et al. 1997 on consistent hashing, recalled, not checked]* U15 owns the relational theory, U9.5 and U10.3 own consistent hashing, U10.6 owns the NoSQL families; the numbers above are specific to the simulated distributions and are labelled so.

**Assignment A16.11** (10 marks; pass at 7/10 with Q4 and Q5 accepted)

**Q1 (1 mark, multiple choice).** Which scaling technique splits data so that each database holds a subset, and cannot fix a single hot key by hashing?

(A) Master-slave replication  
(B) Federation  
(C) Sharding  
(D) Denormalization

**Q2 (2 marks, multiple select; all correct options and no wrong option).** Which statements about scaling the data tier are true?

(A) Adding a node under consistent hashing moves only a small fraction of the keys, where hash mod N moves most of them  
(B) A single-threaded replica applying writes behaves like a queue whose delay grows steeply near full load  
(C) Denormalizing d copies makes an update cost d writes in exchange for cheaper reads  
(D) Master-master replication removes all conflicts

**Q3 (2 marks, numerical answer (times)).** A replica applies writes at a load of 0.9 of its capacity. Federation into three databases cuts the load on the replica for one database to 0.3. How many times shorter is the mean time in system, if it is 1 over mu minus lambda for an M/M/1 queue?

**Q4 (2 marks, prove or derive; every step with its reason).** Show that adding an 11th node moves about 1 in 11 of the keys under consistent hashing but about 10 in 11 under hash mod N.

**Q5 (3 marks, programming).** Implement hash mod N and consistent hashing with virtual nodes, measure the keys moved when adding an 11th node, the load maximum with 1 and 100 virtual nodes, and a hot shard measurement under Zipf load.

<details><summary>Key for A16.11 (open only after your attempt)</summary>

- **Q1:** C. Sharding distributes rows by a key, and one key remains on one shard however good the hash is.
- **Q2:** A, B, C. D is false: both masters accept writes, so conflicts must be resolved.
- **Q3:** 7 times (tolerance ±0.01). At 0.9 the mean time is 10 service times, at 0.3 it is 1.43, and 10 over 1.4286 is 7.
- **Q4 (marking outline):** Under consistent hashing the new node takes over only the arcs it now owns on the ring, which on average is 1 over 11 of the ring, and only keys on those arcs move to it. Under hash mod N a key stays on its server only if its hash has the same remainder mod 10 and mod 11. For a uniform hash that happens for one remainder pair in every 11 equally likely classes, so a fraction 1 over 11 stays and 10 over 11 move, about 91 percent.
- **Q5 (what a passing submission shows):** About 8.3 percent move with the ring and about 91 percent with mod N, the maximum load falls from about 2.2 to about 1.2 times the mean with 100 virtual nodes, and the hottest of 16 shards is about 2.06 times the mean.

</details>

### U16.12 Caching: layers, key choices, and the four update strategies
**Sources:** SDP CACHE
- **Topics:** why cache (shorter page loads, less load on servers and databases, absorbing uneven loads and spikes); where: client caching (the OS or browser), CDN caching, web server caching (reverse proxies and caches such as Varnish), database caching (default settings tuned to a generic load), application caching (in-memory key-value stores such as Memcached and Redis between the application and storage; Redis adds persistence and built-in data structures such as sorted sets and lists; avoid file-based caching because it hampers cloning and autoscaling); what: caching at the database query level (hash the query as the key; expiry is hard because one changed cell invalidates every cached query that might include it) and caching at the object level (assemble the data into a class instance, remove it when the underlying data changes, which also lets workers consume the latest cached object; suggested contents: user sessions, fully rendered web pages, activity streams, user graph data); when to update the cache: cache-aside (the application reads and writes storage and the cache stays passive: on a miss load from the database, add to the cache and return; lazy loading; each miss costs three trips and entries can go stale, limited by a TTL or write-through; a failed node is replaced by an empty one), write-through (the application writes to the cache as the main store and the cache writes synchronously to the data store; reads of just-written data are fast and data is not stale, but writes are slow and most written data might never be read), write-behind or write-back (add or update the cache and write to the store asynchronously; better write performance, risk of data loss if the cache fails first, more complex) and refresh-ahead (refresh recently accessed entries before they expire; lower latency if the access prediction is right, worse if it is wrong); the disadvantages of caches: keeping them consistent with the source of truth by cache invalidation, which is a hard problem, and changing the application.
- **Results:** with Zipf(1.0) requests over 100,000 keys and an LRU cache of 1,000 entries the hit ratio is 0.506; four independent caches behind a random balancer give the same 0.506 each (each holds the same hot keys), while four caches sharded by key behave as one cache of 4,000 entries and reach 0.640, so sharding buys capacity and replication buys only throughput and availability [D, check]; mean latency with a 0.5 ms cache round trip and a 5 ms database read is 1.05 ms at a 90% hit ratio, 3.25 ms at 50% and 0.555 ms at 99% when each miss costs the three cache-aside trips, so the last 10 points of hit ratio are worth more than any cache speed-up [D, check]; in a single-threaded simulation with 10% writes, cache-aside with a 50-operation TTL returned stale data on 2.1% of reads, invalidate-on-write and write-through on none, and write-behind lost the 31 writes not yet flushed when the cache died (races between concurrent readers and writers, which the model leaves out, are why real cache-aside needs more care) [D, check]; the mean staleness after an update with a TTL of T and a uniformly random update time is T/2, so TTLs of 10, 60 and 600 s give 5, 30 and 300 s [D]; a cache cannot make a uniform workload faster: its value comes from skew, so measure the skew first (U10.6 owns the Zipf analysis and U14.9 the hardware caches whose policies are the same) [S].
- **Build:** an LRU cache (U10.6) with the four update strategies as pluggable policies over a simulated database, driven by Zipf and uniform streams with hit ratio, staleness and loss metrics; a sharded cache cluster on the ring of U9.5 and a cluster that loses a node; a cache-aside wrapper for `sqlite3`. [local]
- **Go track:** the caching exercises are written in Go (enter U23.2 and U23.3): the LRU cache, cache-aside with a mutex, and request coalescing for a cache stampede (50 concurrent callers for one key make 1 backend call and 49 share it). [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Nishtala et al. 2013, "Scaling Memcache at Facebook"; cache stampede and request coalescing, recalled, not checked]* the thundering-herd problem (many misses for one hot key at once) is not in the source and is taught as a gap-fill.

**Assignment A16.12** (10 marks; pass at 7/10 with Q4 and Q5 accepted)

**Q1 (1 mark, multiple choice).** With Zipf requests over 100000 keys and an LRU cache of 1000 entries, four caches sharded by key compared with four independent caches behind a random balancer give a hit ratio that is

(A) The same  
(B) Higher, equal to a single cache of 4000 entries  
(C) Lower, because shards split the data  
(D) Zero for the shards

**Q2 (2 marks, multiple select; all correct options and no wrong option).** Which statements about caching are true?

(A) Cache-aside leaves the cache passive and loads on a miss  
(B) Write-behind can lose writes that were not flushed when the cache fails  
(C) A TTL of T with a uniformly random update time gives mean staleness T over 2  
(D) A cache makes a uniform workload much faster

**Q3 (2 marks, numerical answer (ms)).** A cache round trip is 0.5 ms, a database read 5 ms and a miss costs the cache check, the database read and the cache set, three trips. What is the mean latency in ms at a hit ratio of 0.8?

**Q4 (2 marks, prove or derive; every step with its reason).** Show that with a TTL of T seconds and an update at a uniformly random time the mean staleness is T over 2, and give the values for 10, 60 and 600 s.

**Q5 (3 marks, programming).** Simulate cache-aside with a TTL, invalidate on write, write-through and write-behind with 10 percent writes, reporting the stale reads and the lost writes, and an LRU hit ratio experiment for one, four independent and four sharded caches.

<details><summary>Key for A16.12 (open only after your attempt)</summary>

- **Q1:** B. Independent caches each hold the same hot keys so the ratio stays at 0.506, while sharding gives the capacity of 4000 entries and 0.640.
- **Q2:** A, B, C. D is false: the value of a cache comes from skew in the request distribution.
- **Q3:** 1.6 ms (tolerance ±0.01). A hit costs 0.5 ms and a miss costs 0.5 plus 5 plus 0.5 = 6 ms, so 0.4 plus 1.2 = 1.6 ms.
- **Q4 (marking outline):** If the entry was cached at time 0 and expires at T, an update at a uniform time U in the interval 0 to T leaves the cached value stale from U until T, a duration T minus U. The mean of T minus U for uniform U is T over 2. For T equal to 10, 60 and 600 seconds the means are 5, 30 and 300 seconds.
- **Q5 (what a passing submission shows):** Cache-aside with a 50-operation TTL shows about 2 percent stale reads, the invalidating and write-through variants none, write-behind loses the writes not yet flushed, and the hit ratios are about 0.506, 0.506 and 0.640.

</details>

### U16.13 Asynchronism, communication and security basics: queues, back pressure, HTTP, TCP and UDP, RPC and REST
**Sources:** SDP ASYNC, COMM, SEC
- **Topics:** asynchronism (expensive operations out of the request path, and work done in advance such as periodic aggregation): message queues (an application publishes a job and tells the user its status, a worker takes it, processes it and signals completion, while the client may show a small amount of optimistic work; Redis as a simple message broker whose messages can be lost, RabbitMQ with its AMQP protocol and self-managed nodes, Amazon SQS hosted but with higher latency and possible double delivery), task queues (receive tasks with data, run them and deliver results, with scheduling; Celery, mainly for Python), back pressure (a queue that outgrows memory means cache misses and disk reads, so limit the queue size and answer busy), and the disadvantage that cheap or real-time work is better synchronous. Communication: the hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) as a request and response protocol with a verb and a resource, and the verbs GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with their idempotent, safe and cacheable columns; the transmission control protocol (TCP: connection-oriented, handshake, sequence numbers and checksums, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, many open connections costing memory, connection pooling; use it when all data must arrive intact); the user datagram protocol (UDP: connectionless datagrams that may arrive out of order or not at all, broadcast as with DHCP, no congestion control; use it for lowest latency, when late data is worse than lost data, or for your own error correction, as in VoIP, video chat, streaming and games); the remote procedure call (the call chain client program, client stub marshalling the procedure id and arguments, client and server communication modules, server stub unmarshalling and calling the server procedure, the reply in reverse; focused on exposing behaviours, tightly coupled, hard to debug and cache); representational state transfer (a client and server architecture on resources with stateless communication; four qualities: identify resources by a URI, change them through representations (verbs, headers and body), self-descriptive errors (status codes), and HATEOAS; focused on exposing data, usual for public APIs; its disadvantages: awkward when resources are not a simple hierarchy, few verbs, several round trips for nested data, payload bloat as fields grow); the table comparing RPC and REST calls (signup, resign, read a person, read a person's items, add an item, update an item, delete an item); security basics: encrypt in transit and at rest, sanitize all user inputs to prevent XSS and SQL injection, use parameterized queries, apply the principle of least privilege (the depth is in U5.18, U6.7 and U7.7).
- **Results:** PUT and DELETE are idempotent and POST is not, so a client that retries a timed-out request three times leaves a PUT with the same value as one call but a POST with three created resources, which is why a create endpoint needs an idempotency key [D, check]; a queue with arrival rate λ and service rate μ is stable only if λ < μ; with λ = 0.95 and μ = 0.90 per tick, an unbounded queue grew to about 10,000 after 200,000 ticks (λ − μ = 0.05 per tick) while a queue bounded at 50 dropped 5.2% of arrivals (offered load 1.056 gives (λ − μ)/λ = 5.3%), so back pressure turns unbounded delay into explicit, bounded rejection [D, check]; Little's law L = λW sizes everything: 2,000 requests per second at 50 ms in flight is 100 requests, and a connection pool for 2,000 requests per second with a 5 ms query needs 2,000 × 0.005 = 10 connections [D, check]; at-least-once delivery with a 5% duplicate rate gave 1,055 deliveries for 1,000 messages, and an idempotent consumer that remembers message ids applied each exactly once, so "exactly once" is at-least-once plus idempotence [D, check]; TCP's guarantees cost a handshake and head-of-line waiting, which is what UDP-based real-time applications avoid, and QUIC revisits the trade-off (U2.6) [S]; REST and RPC are not exclusive: the usual design is REST at the public edge and RPC inside (the primer's pastebin and Twitter solutions do this) [S].
- **Build:** a bounded task queue with workers and back pressure measured against λ and μ; an idempotent consumer with a seen-set; a small HTTP service in Python's standard library with GET, PUT and POST and an idempotency key, exercised by a retrying client; the RPC-versus-REST mapping of the primer's table implemented both ways over the same in-memory data. [local]
- **Go track:** the queue, back-pressure and worker exercises are written in Go (enter U23.3): a bounded channel as the queue, a worker pool with a concurrency bound (peak exactly 8 of 8) and cancellation when one job fails (11 of 1,000 jobs started), tested under the race detector. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Hohpe and Woolf on messaging patterns; Fielding 2000 on REST; the gRPC and Protocol Buffers documentation, recalled, not checked]* gRPC and GraphQL are named, not built; the security section is thin in the source (it says so), and the basics are extended in D5 to D8.

With a bound the queue is nearly always full, so the service rate sets the throughput at 0.90 per tick, and the fraction of arrivals that cannot be accepted is (0.95 minus 0.90) over 0.95 = 0.0526, about 5.3 percent.
