<details><summary>Key for A14.20 (open only after your attempt)</summary>

- **Q1:** B. The ridge is 25 FLOP/B; below it the bound is I·β = 2 × 400 = 800 GFLOP/s.
- **Q2:** A, B, C. D is false: accuracy usually drops slightly and can drop badly without calibration or quantisation-aware training.
- **Q3:** 8 TFLOP/s (tolerance ±0). The ridge is 20 FLOP/B, so the layer is memory bound at 8 × 1 = 8 TFLOP/s.
- **Q4 (marking outline):** Row i of A enters from the left delayed by i cycles and column j of B from the top delayed by j cycles, and values move one cell per cycle; so A[i][k] and B[k][j] meet in cell (i, j) at cycle i + j + k, and only there; the cell accumulates their product, so after all k it holds the sum over k of A[i][k] B[k][j] = C[i][j]; the last product for cell (i, j) arrives at cycle i + j + K − 1, the largest is at i = j = n − 1, cycle K + 2n − 3, so the array needs K + 2n − 2 cycles counting from cycle 0.
- **Q5 (what a passing submission shows):** Outputs equal to NumPy, cycle counts of K + 2n − 2, utilisation K/(K + 2n − 2), roofline placements that match hand calculations, and measured quantisation error variances within 2% of Δ²/12.

</details>

### U14.21 Quality of service for caches and networks on chip, and emerging directions
**Sources:** MCA W12; ACA o
- **Topics:** Quality of Service for TCMPs: QoS of NoC and Caches in TCMPs (the multicore course's Week 12; the domain-specific-accelerator part of that week is in U14.20): why a shared last-level cache and a shared on-chip network let one application slow another, and how to measure it (slowdown against running alone, weighted speed-up, harmonic speed-up, maximum-to-minimum slowdown as unfairness); cache way-partitioning, utility-based partitioning driven by per-application miss curves, and the greedy marginal-utility allocator; page colouring as a software partition of sets; NoC arbitration for QoS: round-robin, weighted round-robin, age-based and priority arbitration, virtual-channel reservation, and frame-based schemes that give each source a bandwidth share per frame; the relation to network QoS, where the token bucket and fair queueing of U3.6 play the same role between machines that weighted arbitration plays between cores. Emerging Trends in Network On Chips: three-dimensional stacking with through-silicon vias, chiplets joined over an interposer, and photonic and wireless links on chip. In the advanced architecture course's outline, this unit continues "the theory of on-chip networks" of U14.16.
- **Results:** Weighted speed-up is the sum over applications of IPC_shared/IPC_alone and harmonic speed-up is N divided by the sum of IPC_alone/IPC_shared [Def]; with IPCs 2.0 and 1.0 alone and 1.5 and 0.5 shared, the weighted speed-up is 1.25, the harmonic speed-up 0.6 and the unfairness (slowdowns 1.33 and 2) 1.5 [check]; for two applications sharing 16 ways with the stated hit curves, exhaustive search gives the unique optimum of 7 ways and 9 ways at 158 hits per kilo-instruction against 156 for an equal split, and the greedy marginal-utility allocator reaches the same split on these curves, though greedy allocation is not optimal for curves that are not concave [check]; a weighted round-robin arbiter with weights 3 and 1 grants 75% and 25% of cycles under saturation, and a source waits at most the sum of the other weights between grants, which bounds its latency independently of the other source's offered load [P, check]; the algorithms for network QoS themselves (token bucket, generalised processor sharing, fair queueing) are proved in U3.6 and only cited here.
- **Build:** a QoS arbiter (round-robin, weighted round-robin and age-based) added to the NoC simulator of U14.16, and a way-partitioned shared cache added to the cache simulator of U14.8; a mixed workload of one latency-sensitive and one streaming source, reporting the latency-sensitive source's mean and 99th-percentile latency with and without isolation, and the fairness metrics above. Simulation only. [simulator]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Qureshi and Patt (2006) on utility-based cache partitioning; Lee, Ng and Asanović (2008) on globally synchronised frames; Eyerman and Eeckhout (2008) on multiprogram metrics; recalled, not checked]* links to U3.6, which owns the network QoS algorithms.

- **Q2:** A, B, C. D is false: in the unit's example the equal split gives 156 hits per kilo-instruction and the 7 to 9 split gives 158.

- **Q4 (marking outline):** One round grants each source exactly its weight in cycles, so a round has W cycles and source i holds w_i of them; over k rounds the fraction is k w_i/(k W) = w_i/W, and a partial round changes the count by less than W, so the long-run fraction is w_i/W; between the last grant of source i in one round and its first in the next, only the other sources are served, each for its weight, which is W − w_i cycles at most.

### U14.22 Low-power design, reliability and hardware security
**Sources:** ACA W11–12, o
- **Topics:** Week 11: Low power design: dynamic power α C V² f and its terms (activity factor, switched capacitance, supply voltage, clock frequency), static (leakage) power, the end of Dennard scaling and dark silicon; clock gating and power gating; dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and the energy per task, which scales with V², against race-to-idle when leakage is large; power and energy metrics (energy per instruction, energy-delay product); thermal limits. Week 12: Reliability and Hardware Security: transient (soft) faults from particle strikes and permanent faults from wear-out; failure rate, FIT (failures per 10⁹ device-hours) and MTTF; architectural vulnerability factor; error-detecting and error-correcting codes (parity, Hamming single-error correction, SECDED) for caches and memory; redundancy by triple modular redundancy and redundant multithreading. Hardware security from the defender's side: cache timing channels described as an information-flow model (a secret-dependent access changes which set the attacker's probe finds evicted), and defences by partitioning, randomised mapping and constant-time code; trusted execution environments as a hardware boundary. The outline's "aspects of low-power design, hardware security, and reliability" is the scope of this unit; attacks and their deeper defences belong to U5.20 and U6.9.
- **Results:** Scaling V and f together by 0.8 multiplies dynamic power by 0.512 and dynamic energy per task by 0.64 [D, check]; with α = 0.1, C = 50 nF, V = 1 V and f = 3 GHz the dynamic power is 15 W [check]; in the stated example with leakage 2 W at 1 V, running a 3 × 10⁹-cycle task slowly at 1.5 GHz and 0.7 V uses 10.15 J against 17.1 J for race-to-idle over the same 2 s window, and the comparison reverses when leakage dominates [check]; a Hamming code needs r check bits with 2^r ≥ m + r + 1, so 7 for 64 data bits and 10 for 512, and SECDED adds one overall parity bit, giving the (72, 64) code with 12.5% overhead against 11 bits (2.1%) for a 512-bit line [P, check]; the (72, 64) SECDED decoder corrects every single-bit error and detects every double-bit error in randomised trials [check]; failure rates of independent parts add in a series system, so 64 Mbit at 1000 FIT per Mbit is 64 000 FIT and an MTTF of 15 625 hours [D, check]; triple modular redundancy has reliability 3R² − 2R³, which is 0.972 at R = 0.9 but worse than one module below R = 0.5, and its MTTF is 5/(6λ), less than a single module's 1/λ [D, check]; in the cache-channel model the attacker's observation identifies the secret's set index without partitioning and is independent of the secret with a static partition [check].
- **Build:** a Hamming SECDED encoder and decoder for a 64-bit word and a 512-bit cache line, with fault injection and a report of corrected, detected and silent outcomes; a power-model explorer that sweeps V and f under a stated leakage model and finds the energy-optimal operating point for a task with a deadline; a simulated prime-and-probe model on the cache simulator of U14.8, with and without way partitioning (defensive measurement on synthetic data only, never against real systems). Hardware power counters (for example `powermetrics` on macOS) are optional and not required. [local] [simulator]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Hamming (1950); Hsiao (1970) on SECDED codes; Mukherjee et al. (2003) on the architectural vulnerability factor; Esmaeilzadeh et al. (2011) on dark silicon; Kocher et al. (2019) on Spectre; recalled, not checked]* links to U6.9 and U5.20, which own attacks and defences; leakage in the explorer is modelled as proportional to V, a stated simplification.

- **Q1:** B. Dynamic power scales as V²f, so 0.9² × 0.8 = 0.81 × 0.8 = 0.648.
- **Q2:** A, B, D. C is false: the MTTF of TMR is 5/(6λ), shorter than 1/λ, although its reliability is higher for missions shorter than about 0.69/λ.
- **Q3:** 15625 hours (tolerance ±0.5). Rates add in series, so the total is 64 000 FIT, 64 000 failures per 10^9 hours, and the MTTF is 10^9/64 000 = 15 625 hours.
- **Q4 (marking outline):** The syndrome has r bits and must name each of the m + r single-error positions and the no-error case, so 2^r ≥ m + r + 1 is necessary; placing check bits at the powers of two and letting check bit p cover the positions whose index has bit p set makes the syndrome equal to the error position, so the bound suffices; with an overall parity bit, a single error flips overall parity and is corrected by the syndrome, while a double error leaves overall parity unchanged but gives a non-zero syndrome, so it is detected and not miscorrected.
- **Q5 (what a passing submission shows):** All single errors corrected and all double errors detected over at least 10 000 injected faults, check-bit counts of 8 and 11, and an explorer whose dynamic-power figures match α C V² f and whose optimum moves towards race-to-idle as leakage grows.

</details>


# PART G. CAPSTONES

## D13. Capstones

Aim: ten integrating projects, each one drawing on units from several domains, each built from your own components first and then checked against standard tools. A capstone has no weekly assignment; it is accepted against the listed criteria, with the Master Rules' tutor stance applied (the tutor does not write graded work). Each is local first, labelled with its cost, and, wherever it touches security, confined to the laboratory rules of U6.1.

### U13.1 Capstone: a user-space TCP/IP stack over a lossy virtual link
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: Ethernet framing, ARP, IPv4 with checksum and optional fragmentation, ICMP echo, UDP, a DNS stub, and TCP with the three-way handshake, cumulative acknowledgments, a sliding window, retransmission with the RFC 6298 timer, fast retransmit, Reno-style congestion control, and a socket-like API; the virtual link in DSim has configurable delay, loss, reordering, duplication and bandwidth. Draws on U2.2 to U2.14, U3.3 to U3.5 and U9.1.
- **Results:** The measured throughput on a lossy link is consistent with the Mathis estimate MSS/(RTT·√(2p/3))·C up to a constant [D, to be shown by experiment]; the stack passes a conformance suite of at least thirty scripted scenarios, including simultaneous open and close, window probes, and recovery from a lost final ACK [Def].
- **Build:** the stack, the scenario suite, a throughput-versus-loss experiment with a plot, a packet-capture writer producing a file readable by Wireshark, and a ten-line report on where the stack departs from the RFCs. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Stevens, TCP/IP Illustrated; RFC 9293, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: your stack interoperates with the operating system's TCP through a loopback tunnel in the lab only.

### U13.2 Capstone: a secure channel from your own primitives (never deployed)
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: an authenticated key exchange (ephemeral ECDH from U5.15, signatures from U5.17, HKDF from U5.18) followed by an AEAD record layer (U5.7 and U5.11) with sequence numbers, replay protection, key rotation and a downgrade-resistant version field, running over your stack of U13.1 or over loopback sockets. Draws on D5 and D2.
- **Results:** The channel resists a scripted adversary that tampers, replays, reorders, truncates and downgrades, and the negative test suite shows each rejection [Def]; a written threat model states what the channel does not protect (metadata, traffic analysis, side channels) [Def].
- **Build:** the implementation, the negative test suite, a comparison of handshake cost and record overhead with TLS 1.3 from the `ssl` module on loopback, and the explicit statement that the code is for learning and is never deployed (Master Rules 6.8 and 11.1). [local; learning only]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Noise Protocol Framework; RFC 8446, recalled, not checked]* acceptance includes one real flaw you introduce on purpose and then find with your own tests.

### U13.3 Capstone: a replicated, sharded key-value store with fault injection
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: shards by consistent hashing (U9.5), each shard a Raft group (U9.14), a router, optional multi-shard transactions by two-phase commit (U9.18), a Jepsen-style nemesis (partitions, crashes, clock skew, message loss) in DSim, a linearizability checker (U9.16), and metrics with an SLO (U12.1). Draws on D9, D10 and D12.
- **Results:** No linearizability violation appears over at least 10,000 randomised schedules with the nemesis active; availability under a minority partition is measured and reported against the theory [Def]; a deliberately broken variant (for example a stale-read optimisation) is caught by the checker [Def].
- **Build:** the store, the nemesis, the checker run, a latency and availability report, and a design note on what would change for geo-distribution. [local]
- **Go track:** the capstone is written in Go (enter U23.3, U23.5, U23.6 and U23.7): the consistent-hash ring for sharding, the write-ahead-logged store for each replica, goroutines and channels for the replicas with a fault injector, and a reconciliation loop that restarts crashed replicas; acceptance is `go test -race` plus the fault-injection checks of this unit. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kingsbury's Jepsen reports; Ongaro's thesis, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: the report states the exact seeds so any failure replays.

### U13.4 Capstone: an end-to-end data platform from your own engines
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: ingestion into your Kafka-like log (U11.6), a stream job with event-time windows and sketches (U11.7), a batch job on your mini-MapReduce or mini-Spark (U11.3, U11.4) computing aggregates and PageRank (U11.11) from the same log, a serving store (U10.4 or U10.5), lineage, data-quality checks, and a cost model. Draws on D10 and D11.
- **Results:** The end-to-end effect is exactly-once across a crash of any single component, shown by an invariant such as the conservation of a sum; skew in the key distribution is detected and mitigated; the streaming and batch answers agree after late data is accounted for [Def].
- **Build:** the pipeline, the crash and skew experiments, the reconciliation report, and a comparison of one stage with its cloud counterpart (U12.2) by cost and latency. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kleppmann Ch.10–12; the kappa architecture, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: a single command reproduces the run from a seed.

### U13.5 Capstone: a small service on Google Cloud with identity, networking, reliability and cost controls
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: a reference architecture for a small web service: a virtual network with subnets and firewall rules (U4.8), least-privilege identities (U7.7), an HTTP load balancer, managed compute (U4.7), object storage and a database (U10.7), monitoring with SLOs and burn-rate alerts (U12.1), a budget alert, labels, and a verified teardown; infrastructure described as code and checked by a policy linter built from U7.5 and U8.6. Draws on D4, D7, D10 and D12.
- **Results:** The plan passes your policy linter (no public storage, no wildcard roles, no unrestricted ingress except the load balancer's port) and your cost estimate from the live price list stays below the lab budget; the SLO and its alerts are validated against a simulated load [Def].
- **Build:** the design document, the infrastructure code, the linter report, the cost estimate, and, only if the budget allows and a personal lab project is used (never a work account), an applied deployment with a screenshot-free teardown log showing the project returned to zero resources. [plan only; credit if applied]
- **Go track:** the capstone service is written in Go (enter U23.4 and U23.7): the twelve-factor service with a health endpoint, structured logs and graceful shutdown, packaged by the multi-stage Dockerfile for deployment to the platform; the build and the termination-signal test were run, the image build and the cloud deployment were not (no container daemon and no cloud access in the build environment). [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: the platform's architecture framework, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: the same-day teardown rule of the course profile is met.

### U13.6 Capstone: a security programme for a synthetic organisation
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: for a fictional company you define, produce: a quantitative risk register with Monte Carlo loss exceedance (U8.2 and U8.3), an ATT&CK coverage map and a D3FEND control selection (U7.2, U7.4), a kill-chain analysis of two scenarios (U7.3), a STIX bundle of synthetic indicators shared over your TAXII server (U7.6), a STIG-style baseline and compliance report (U7.5), policies with a conflict check (U8.6), an incident-response plan and business-continuity plan with recovery objectives (U8.4), a resilience simulation (U8.5), a privacy section with a data map, a GDPR and DPDP obligation map and a differentially private release of one statistic (U8.8 and U8.9), a cryptographic inventory and a post-quantum migration plan (U5.25), and a one-page board summary. Draws on D5 to D8.
- **Results:** The programme's numbers trace to code (every figure in the board summary is produced by a script from the register); the control portfolio is justified by the knapsack optimiser of U8.3; every external statement (a law, a standard, a framework version) carries its source and the date it was checked [Def].
- **Build:** the artefacts above, a reproducible build script, and a short critique of the programme's weakest assumption. All data is synthetic and no real organisation or person is analysed. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: NIST CSF 2.0 profiles; ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: the board summary is readable by a non-specialist in five minutes.

### U13.7 Capstone: a multicore simulator (pipeline, caches, coherence and a NoC) running a parallel kernel
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: assemble the models of D14 into one cycle-level simulator of a small tiled multicore and run a parallel kernel on it: an AArch64-subset or RISC-V-subset instruction model (U14.2) and a pipelined core with forwarding and branch prediction (U14.4 to U14.6), optionally out of order (U14.7); private L1 caches and a shared, banked last-level cache with replacement and write policies (U14.8 and U14.9) and a TLB and page walker (U14.10); a DRAM controller with a stated timing model (U14.11); MESI or a directory protocol checked by the model checker of U14.14; a memory-model mode whose litmus-test outcomes match the enumerator of U14.15; and a mesh NoC with XY routing and virtual channels (U14.16). The kernel is a parallel reduction or a tiled matrix multiply with a lock or barrier (U14.13), run on 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 cores. Draws on U14.2 to U14.16 and, for speed-up analysis, U11.1.
- **Results:** Each component is validated against its unit's oracle before integration (the effective-access-time formula of U4.1, the coherence model checker, the litmus enumerator, the channel-dependency-graph deadlock check and the analytic NoC metrics) [check]; the measured speed-up curve is explained by a breakdown of cycles into compute, cache misses, coherence traffic and NoC contention, and compared with Amdahl's and Gustafson's predictions from U11.1 [Def]; the kernel's result is identical to a NumPy reference on every configuration [check].
- **Build:** the simulator as small modules with one test suite per component and an integration suite, configuration files for each experiment, a reproducible script that regenerates every figure, and a short critique of the model's least realistic assumption. Runs on the Mac's CPU in Python, with an optional C port of the inner loop compiled with `clang`. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: gem5 and Sniper as reference simulators; Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach; Sorin, Hill and Wood, A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence; recalled, not checked]* acceptance: every number in the report is produced by a script, and a reviewer can rerun any experiment from its configuration file.

### U13.8 Capstone: a small relational database engine checked against sqlite3
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: build, from your own code, a single-node relational engine and check it against the reference engine in Python's `sqlite3` module: a slotted-page heap file with a buffer pool (U15.14 and U15.15); a B+-tree index on the primary key and one secondary index (U15.16); a parser for a SQL subset (create table, insert, select with where, join, group by and order by; U15.7 and U15.8) that produces a relational-algebra tree (U15.5); a rule-based and then cost-based optimiser with selection and projection push-down and a join-order search by dynamic programming (U15.17 and U15.18); iterator operators including an external merge sort and a hash join; strict two-phase locking with a lock table and wait-for-graph deadlock detection (U15.20 to U15.22); and a write-ahead log with redo and undo recovery (U15.23). A normalisation helper reads functional dependencies and reports keys and the BCNF decomposition (U15.11 and U15.12). Draws on U15.1 to U15.23 and, for the optional replicated mode, U15.26 and U9.17.
- **Results:** Every query in a generated suite of at least 1,000 random queries over random tables returns the same multiset of rows as sqlite3 [check]; the index scan and the sequential scan return the same answer and the page-access counts follow the formulas of U15.16 and U15.17 (a B+-tree of 10^6 keys with order 200 is 3 levels high) [check]; the chosen join order is the cheapest of the enumerated ones and matches an exhaustive search on queries of up to five relations [check]; histories executed by concurrent client threads are conflict serializable by the test of U15.21, deadlocks are found and one victim is aborted [check]; after a crash injected at each log position the recovered tables hold exactly the committed transactions' effects [check].
- **Build:** the engine as small modules (storage, index, parser, algebra, optimiser, executor, locks, log) with a test suite per module and a differential tester against sqlite3, a script that prints the plan and page-access counts for any query, and a short critique of what the engine leaves out (the full SQL language, statistics, MVCC, media recovery). Runs in Python on the Mac's CPU; only invented data is used. [local]
- **Go track:** the capstone engine is written in Go (enter U23.5 and U23.2): storage on the checksummed log, a SQL subset behind the `database/sql` driver interface, transactions as in the driver of U23.5, and an oracle check against `sqlite3` run by a Python script on the exported query results. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: SQLite's own file format and the CMU 15-445 BusTub project and the Berkeley Minibase course as comparable teaching engines; Garcia-Molina, Ullman and Widom, Database Systems: The Complete Book, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: a reviewer can rerun the differential tester with a different seed and the suite still agrees with sqlite3.

### U13.9 Capstone: a design dossier and a working miniature of a large-scale service
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: choose one service from the eight worked designs of U16.14 to U16.16 or from the additional questions of U16.16 (a rate limiter, a chat service, a feed, a file sync service), then produce two things: a design dossier in the four-step template of U16.8 (use cases and assumptions, estimates with every figure shown, a high-level design, core components with data model and API, and a scaling plan with the bottleneck named at each stage), and a working miniature in Python at the primer's rates scaled down: the data store (U16.11 and U15), a cache with a stated update strategy (U16.12), a queue with back pressure and an idempotent consumer (U16.13), shards placed by consistent hashing with virtual nodes (U16.11 and U9.5), a load balancer and replicas (U16.9), a failure injector (U9.17), and a load generator with a Zipf key distribution (U10.6). The dossier names the patterns used (U16.2 to U16.6) and gives each design choice with the alternative rejected and why. Draws on U16.1 to U16.16 and, for the optional cloud deployment, U4.7, U4.8, U10.7 and U12.1 to U12.3.
- **Results:** the estimates in the dossier recompute from the stated assumptions to within 5 percent (the primer's own errors, U16.8 and U16.10, are not copied) [check]; under the generated load the miniature's measured hit ratio, queue length, shard imbalance and tail latency are reported next to the dossier's predictions, with each difference explained [check]; with an injected failure of a shard, a replica and the cache the service keeps answering within its stated availability target, and the report shows the fraction of requests that failed or were stale [check]; a duplicate-delivery test shows each message applied exactly once and a queue-overload test shows rejection instead of unbounded delay [check]; at least two design choices are reversed in a second run (for example sharded against independent caches, push against pull fan-out) and the measured difference is compared with the unit's figures [check].
- **Build:** the dossier as one document with numbered assumptions and a table of estimates, the miniature as small modules with a test per module and a single script that runs the load, injects the failures and prints the report, and a one-page critique of what the miniature leaves out (real networks, concurrency races, multi-datacentre operation, security). Runs in Python on the Mac's CPU with invented data only; an optional deployment on Google Cloud is labelled with its cost and torn down after the test. [local]
- **Go track:** the working miniature is written in Go (enter U23.3, U23.4 and U23.6): the design dossier names the components, and the miniature builds the ring, the limiter, the cache and the service skeleton from the reference programs; acceptance is `go test -race` and the load numbers the dossier predicted. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, and Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, as comparable reading; recalled, not checked]* acceptance: a reviewer can change one assumption, such as the read-to-write ratio, rerun the estimator and the miniature, and find both move in the predicted direction.

### U13.10 Capstone: an analytics pipeline from raw data to a decision, with the statistics, the model, the sketches and the distributed run built from scratch
**Sources:** none (capstone; assembles earlier units)
- **Topics:** Scope: choose a decision problem with a synthetic data generator you write yourself (customer churn for a subscription service, fraud in card transactions, or demand and inventory for a small retailer), then deliver an end-to-end pipeline and a written decision memo. The pipeline has seven stages. (1) Data and preprocessing: a generator with a known ground truth, deliberately messy output (missing values, duplicates, outliers, a skewed class), a cleaning step and a documented preprocessing plan (U19.2, U19.11, U21.1). (2) Exploration and inference: descriptive statistics, confidence intervals by formula and by bootstrap, a two-sample test and an ANOVA on the segments, with a multiple-testing correction (U19.3 to U19.6). (3) Models: a regression and a classifier built from scratch (normal equations, IRLS logistic regression, a CART tree, a naive Bayes or k-NN baseline) and one association-rule or sequence-mining result (U19.7 to U19.13, U18.6), compared by cross-validation, the ROC curve and a cost-aware threshold (U19.8, U19.13). (4) A Bayesian version of the main model with a hand-written sampler, priors justified, convergence reported, and a Bayes factor or leave-one-out comparison with the frequentist one (U19.14 to U19.17). (5) Linear-algebra and graph components: a low-rank or PCA step, a recommendation or completion step on the user–item matrix, and a graph measure on a customer or transaction graph (U18.3 to U18.8, U17.11 to U17.13). (6) Scale: the same pipeline on 10³ times more data using a Count-Min sketch for frequencies, a Bloom filter for deduplication, MinHash for near-duplicate customers, and a two-phase map-reduce aggregation on the miniature framework, with bytes moved reported (U20.2 to U20.8, U17.5, U15.17); the storage side uses the database of D15 with an index chosen by measurement (U15.16). (7) Decision: the memo states the expected cost and benefit of the recommended policy with an interval, the assumptions that would reverse it, and the checks that guard against the usual failures (leakage, survivorship, multiple comparisons, class imbalance).
- **Results:** the recovered effects match the generator's ground truth within the reported intervals on at least 90 percent of repeated runs with fresh seeds [check]; the from-scratch regression, logistic regression and tree agree with the library versions (scikit-learn or SciPy) to the stated tolerances [check]; the sampler's R-hat is below 1.01 and its posterior means agree with the closed-form or grid answer where one exists [check]; the sketch-based frequencies stay inside their stated error bounds and the sketched pipeline's decision agrees with the exact pipeline's on the full data [check]; the pipeline is reproducible from one command and one seed [check]; the memo's cost figure recomputes from the stated assumptions to within 5 percent [check].
- **Build:** a package with one module per stage and a test per module, a single `run_pipeline` script with a seed argument, a notebook that regenerates every figure, and the two-page memo. Runs locally in Python on the Mac's CPU with invented data only; an optional run of the scaled stage on a managed cluster service (U12.3) is labelled with its cost and torn down after the test. [local]
- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: the capstone pattern of U13.1 to U13.9; Provost and Fawcett, Data Science for Business, and Gelman et al., Regression and Other Stories, as comparable reading, recalled, not checked]* acceptance: a reviewer can change one assumption (the churn rate, the cost of a false negative, the data size) and find that the memo, the models and the sketches move in the predicted direction, and the work is accepted against the Master Rules' tutor stance with no graded work written by the tutor. On demand: U17.4, U17.5 and U17.16 for the data structures of the pipeline.

The line numbers for DAP, AGDS, SDS, DBMS, BDA, ALA, DM and DSAD refer to `src5.txt`, a verbatim copy of `data-analytics.txt` (356 lines). The file holds nine outlines; the ninth, Big Data Computing, is an exact duplicate of BDC (checked line by line against `cloud-computing.txt`) and has no cells of its own. The DBMS course is a fourth database course and its cells are cited by the existing D15 units. For DM the file gives only the instructor's name and the outline text, so its title is inferred.

The line numbers for ISE and SEM refer to `src6.txt`, a verbatim copy of `software-engineering.txt` (87 lines, two outlines). Anomalies in it are listed in Appendix E.1.

## Appendix C. Prerequisite bridges and the prerequisites the sources state

### C.1 Bridge units (each is taught immediately before the first unit that needs it)

| Bridge | Concept taught | Needed by |
|---|---|---|
| U1.2 | Linux shell, scripting, Python for systems work, regular expressions and Git | every lab from U1.3 on, the byte-level work of U2.3, and the shell and language prerequisites listed for the Google Cloud course (shell scripting, one programming language, SQL; SQL itself is bridged in U10.1) |
| U2.1 | probability, random processes and queueing for networks | U2.2 (statistical multiplexing, delay), U2.13 (ALOHA), U3.3 (head-of-line blocking), U3.6 (scheduling), U4.7 (autoscaling), U12.1 (SLO arithmetic) |
| U2.7 | graph algorithms for routing — shortest paths, spanning trees and distributed relaxation | U2.9 (routing protocols), U2.12 (spanning tree protocol), U3.7 (controller path computation), U4.6 (traffic engineering), U9.11 (distributed minimum spanning tree) |
| U2.11 | coding theory — GF(2), polynomial division, CRC and Hamming codes | U2.12 (error control); reused in U5.5 (GF(2⁸)) and U5.6 (LFSR as polynomial division) |
| U3.1 | lookup data structures — tries, hashing and Bloom filters | U3.4 (IP lookup), U3.5 (classification), U3.11–U3.12 (NDN tables); reused in U10.4 (Cassandra) and U10.5 (HBase) |
| U3.2 | bipartite matching, Hall's theorem and Birkhoff–von Neumann decomposition | U3.3 (switch scheduling) and U3.10 (Clos networks) |
| U4.1 | operating systems and computer architecture for virtualization | U4.2 (virtualization), U4.4 (containers), U9.x (process and thread models) |
| U4.5 | network flows and linear programming | U4.6 (B4 and SWAN allocation), U3.6 (max–min fairness), U11.9 (optimisation in ML) |
| U5.1 | probability, entropy and asymptotics for cryptography | U5.3 (perfect secrecy, entropy of language), U5.9 (advantage and distinguishers), U5.10 (birthday bound), U5.12 onward (error probabilities) |
| U5.8 | computational complexity, one-way functions and the reduction method | U5.9 onward (every proof of security is a reduction). Addresses the stated prerequisite of the provable-security course: exposure to discrete mathematics, algorithms and theory of computation |
| U5.12 | number theory for public-key cryptography — Fermat, Euler, CRT, quadratic residues, Legendre and Jacobi symbols, primality testing and factoring | U5.13 (discrete log and DDH), U5.14 (RSA, Rabin, ElGamal), U5.15 (curve point counting), U5.17 onward. Continues U5.2 (Euclid and inverses) and U5.5 (groups) |
| U8.2 | quantitative risk — frequency and severity models, Monte Carlo loss exceedance, Bayesian updating and decision under uncertainty | U8.3 (risk management), U8.5 (resilience assessment), U13.6 (security programme capstone). Builds on U5.1 |
| U9.17 | transactions — ACID, serializability, locking, logging and recovery | U9.18 (atomic commit, Percolator, Spanner), U10.5 (Bigtable), U10.7 (managed databases). Builds on U10.1's relational view if read in order, and is self-contained otherwise. The relational and storage background is domain D15 (U15.20 to U15.23 develop the same theory in full, citing the theorems proved here); this unit is the compact version |
| U10.1 | the relational model, SQL, indexing and query processing | U10.4 onward (every store here is defined by what it gives up relative to a relational database), U12.2 (BigQuery). Addresses the SQL prerequisite stated in the cloud-platform source and the database prerequisite stated in the big-data source. Full treatment is in domain D15 (U15.4 to U15.18), read before D10 in the default order; this unit stays as the compact version for a reader who skips D15 |
| U11.8 | machine-learning foundations for scalable learning | U11.9 (machine learning on the engines), U12.3 (machine learning on the cloud platform). A compact version of the foundations; the full treatment is in the earlier unified machine-learning curriculum |
| U11.10 | Markov chains, eigenvectors and PageRank | U11.11 (graph processing). Builds on the random-walk material of U9.2 |
| U14.1 | binary representation, number systems and digital logic | U14.2 (instruction encoding, sign extension), U14.4 (adders, multipliers, IEEE 754), U14.5 (datapath, control state machines), U14.6 (pipeline registers and clocked timing), and every later D14 simulator built from gates and flip-flops. It is the prerequisite the sources state ("a basic understanding of digital logic") |
| U15.3 | sets, relations, functions and first-order logic for the relational model, algebra and calculus | U15.4 to U15.6 (relations as sets of tuples, the algebra and the calculus), U15.11 (functional dependencies as logical statements and the proofs about them) and U15.13 (dependencies as constraints). The sources state discrete mathematics as a prerequisite; this unit supplies it |
| U15.14 | the external-memory model, disks and the cost of sorting | U15.15 to U15.18 (file organisation, indexes, and the costs of query processing and optimisation count page transfers, not instructions), and later U10.2 (distributed file systems) and U11.1 (external sorting in MapReduce) |
| U15.19 | directed graphs, cycles, topological order and partial orders for schedules, deadlocks and timestamps | U15.21 (precedence graphs and serial orders), U15.22 (wait-for graphs, deadlock detection and the timestamp orders of wait-die, wound-wait and timestamp ordering) and U15.23 (the dependency order of log records). U2.7 taught shortest paths and spanning trees; it did not teach cycles and topological order, which are needed here |
| U16.1 | object-oriented programming, UML and design principles for the pattern units | U16.2 to U16.7, and every capstone that builds a program of more than one file |
| U17.1 | discrete mathematics for algorithm analysis: induction, sums, logarithms, recurrences and probability | U17.2 to U17.17 |
| U17.2 | Introduction to algorithms and their analysis: time complexity, asymptotics, merge sort, recurrences and clever linear-time algorithms | U17.3 to U17.17 and every unit whose Results state a running time or an operation count (U2.7, U3.4, U15.17, U15.18, U20.1) |
| U17.3 | Divide and conquer: the master method, quicksort, randomised quicksort, half-majority, multiplication and inversions | U11.3 and U15.17 (the sort inside the shuffle and inside external sorting), U18.9 (the FFT is divide and conquer), U17.4 and every recursive algorithm |
| U17.4 | Heaps, sorting in linear time and order statistics | U11.3 (sort and shuffle), U11.7 (top-k with a heap), U15.17 (external merge sort), U17.12 (the priority queue of Dijkstra) |
| U17.5 | Hashing: hash functions, open addressing and perfect hashing | U3.1 (hashing and Bloom filters), U9.5 and U10.3 (consistent hashing), U15.15 (hashed files), U15.17 (hash joins), U11.3 (the partitioner), U16.7 (the hash map exercise), U20.2 and U20.3 (universal hashing and sketches) |
| U17.6 | Abstract data types, stacks and queues, range queries and the grid-distance problem | U16.7 (the LRU cache), U14.9 (replacement policies), U11.7 (windows), U17.11 (the queue of breadth-first search) |
| U17.7 | Search trees: binary search trees, balancing and red-black trees | U15.16 (B-trees and B+-trees are search trees with wide nodes), U10.5 (sorted tables), U3.4 (lookup trees), U17.16 |
| U17.8 | Augmenting data structures, fixed-universe successor and the van Emde Boas tree, with the geometric primitives | U3.5 (range queries over rules), U17.9 and U17.16 |
| U17.9 | Disjoint sets, amortised analysis and more computational geometry | U17.10 (Kruskal's algorithm uses union–find), U2.7 and U9.11 (spanning trees), and every amortised bound in the curriculum |
| U17.10 | Greedy algorithms, dynamic programming, graphs and minimum spanning trees | U2.7 (spanning trees), U14.9 (Belady's MIN is a greedy rule), U15.18 (dynamic programming over join orders), U16.15 (the ranking designs), U17.17 |
| U17.11 | Graph search: breadth-first and depth-first search, bipartiteness, DFS trees and articulation points | U2.7, U2.12 (the spanning tree protocol), U11.10 and U11.11 (graph traversal and PageRank), U15.19 and U15.21 (cycle detection in schedules), U16.15 (the web crawler), U21.5 |
| U17.12 | Single-source shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford and their applications | U2.7 and U2.9 (path computation in OSPF and BGP), U3.10 (data-centre routing), U11.11 (graph processing), U16.15 |
| U17.13 | All-pairs shortest paths: Floyd–Warshall and Johnson | U2.7, U11.11 and U18.3 (graphs and matrices) |
| U17.14 | Flow networks, the Ford–Fulkerson method, and an introduction to computational complexity | U3.2, U4.5 and U4.6 (matching, flows and traffic engineering), U5.8 (complexity and reductions), U17.17 |

55 bridge units in all. In D17 every unit is an on-demand bridge (the entry map in its introduction lists the units that call on it), which is why D17 appears here in full. Several other units (U5.2 modular arithmetic, U5.5 algebra, U9.1 models and the simulator, U9.2 tail bounds) also begin from first principles and carry source citations as well.

## Appendix D. Gap-fills, candidates not added, and decisions needed

### D.1 What was added beyond the outlines (and why)

- **Prerequisite bridges** (Appendix C.1): required by the instruction to wire prerequisites in just before the concept that demands them.
- **U4.8** (cloud networking on Google Cloud): the thin GCF weeks 5 and 6 name networking products; the concepts underneath are derived from scratch so the product names are replaceable.
- **GCF weeks with title-only outlines** are treated as *inferred*: the concepts under each product name are taught from first principles and the product lens sits next to the concept it implements (compute D4, networking U4.8, identity U7.7, storage U10.7, operations and analytics D12).
- **D16** (software and system design, 2026-11-06): added on request from three public sources (the System Design Primer, the python-patterns collection and the Gang of Four catalogue). Bridge U16.1 (object-oriented design, UML, SOLID) was added before the pattern units. Where an existing unit already owns the theory (DNS U2.4, CDN U3.11, CAP U9.16, nines U9.13, consistent hashing U9.5, NoSQL and caches U10.6, Kafka U11.6, hardware caches U14.9, relational theory D15), D16 keeps the engineering view and points back; the pointers were added to those units.
- **D17 to D21** (the data-analytics extension, 2026-11-06): eight new courses from `data-analytics.txt` gave four new domains, D17 (algorithms and data structures, taught on demand with an entry map and three added units, U17.15 to U17.17), D18 (applied linear algebra), D19 (statistics, data mining and Bayesian analysis) and D20 (scalable data science); the DBMS course was mapped onto the existing D15 units with no new unit. D21 (on-demand prerequisites: Python, school mathematics, scientific Python in place of R, proofs, graph theory, probability) consolidates every prerequisite the sources state or assume, taught in depth with from-scratch builds and assignments, and U13.10 (an analytics pipeline) was added as a capstone. Ownership rules: D15 owns database theory, U11.3 and U11.4 own MapReduce and Spark, U11.7 owns the stream-sketch idea, U11.8 and U11.10 own the compact machine-learning and Markov-chain bridges; D17 to D20 add the analysis, the proofs and the experiments, and the existing units point to them.
- **D22 and D23** (software engineering and Go on demand, 2026-11-06): `software-engineering.txt` holds two NPTEL outlines (ISE, Introduction to Software Engineering, Dhanbad; SEM, Software Engineering, Kharagpur), merged into D22 (14 units, U22.1 to U22.14: life cycle and process models, planning and estimation, scheduling and configuration management, requirements, formal specification, design, structured and object-oriented analysis and design, three units of testing and debugging, maintenance and agile methods, and reliability). U22.14 (software reliability) is a gap-fill from Shooman's book, which the Dhanbad outline lists but ties to no week. D23 (Go, taught on demand, 8 units U23.1 to U23.8) holds the language that the system-design, database-coding and cloud-computing exercises are written in; its programs are in the `go/` module of the work archive, standard library only, with tests run under the race detector (`verify/v_go.out`).
- **Language policy** (2026-11-06): Python is the default language of every Build. Go is the language for three kinds of exercise: system design (D16), database coding (D15, D10 and capstone U13.8) and cloud computing (D4, D9, D11, D12 and capstones U13.3, U13.5 and U13.9). Each such unit carries a **Go track** line naming the Go unit to enter on demand and the result to reproduce; the Python build stays as the oracle where one exists.
- **Capstones** (D13) assemble the earlier units and are not sourced.

### D.3 Decisions I need from you

1. **Labs list.** The GCF outline says the course has 26 labs on Qwiklabs but does not list them. The Build lines give a lab for each concept instead. If you can supply the list, I will map each lab to a unit.
2. **Gap candidates** in D.2: add any, none or all.
3. **Merging with the earlier file.** `unified_curriculum.md` (mathematics, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs) and this file share a method. Merge into one document, or keep two linked by U11.8, U9.2, U5.1 and U14.20? (The merge is planned as a separate, optional step and has not been done.)
4. **Institution of the GCF course.** The file's header says IIT Guwahati while the course block names IIT Kharagpur (Appendix E). Which should the record carry?
5. **Lab environment.** The architecture labs are based on your Apple silicon MacBook (decided 2026-11-04). The security units still assume an isolated host-only VM network you own: tell me the VM tool you use on the Mac and I will adjust those Build lines and cost tags.
6. **C and C++ for DS.** The source asks for C or C++; the curriculum uses Python. Say if you want selected builds ported.
7. **Tooling choices.** The from-scratch guideline leaves tools to the unit; each Build line names its choice. Tell me if any should change.
8. **File name, recorded.** The architecture courses came from `cloud-computing2.txt`, a file whose name says cloud but which holds six computer-architecture courses; they are D14 here. Rename the file if you want the name to match its contents.

9. **Database file, recorded (2026-11-05).** `dbms.txt` holds three database courses, now D15 (printed between D9 and D10). The garbled part of its text layer was re-joined by hand (Appendix E.1); say if you would rather supply a clean copy so the line numbers can point at the original.
10. **Design sources, recorded (2026-11-06).** The company architectures and engineering blogs listed in the primer, and the Anki decks, were not opened or summarised (U16.16 says so); say if you want selected ones added as units. The primer's solutions are one reasonable answer each, taught here with every figure recomputed.
11. **R replaced by Python, recorded (2026-11-06).** The Bayesian course teaches with R, brms and Stan. On the user's instruction every R-related part was converted to Python: U21.3 teaches scientific Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, patsy and statsmodels, Matplotlib) in place of the R programming prerequisite, and U19.15 to U19.17 use PyMC, Bambi and ArviZ, which are installed in the workspace and were run (versions in `verify/v_f7.py`). The source names (R programming, brms, Stan) are kept only where the unit says what replaces them.
12. **Textbook checks, recorded (2026-11-06).** The contents lists of MMDS, CLRS, Strang, Hammack, the Python tutorial and the NCERT mathematics chapters were read from public pages (Appendix F); the other benchmarks of D17 to D21 are recalled, not checked. The Netflix Prize figures in U18.8 were read from public write-ups.
13. **Algorithms and data structures on demand, recorded (2026-11-06).** On the user's instruction D17 is entered the way the prerequisite bridges are: from the unit that needs it. Each of U17.2 to U17.14 begins with a "Bridge for:" line, the introduction of D17 holds the entry map, the Gap-fills of 37 using units name the U17 unit to enter, and three units were added, U17.15 (arrays, linked lists, recursion, binary search, elementary sorts, bit tricks), U17.16 (tries, B-trees, skip lists, string matching) and U17.17 (backtracking, branch and bound, approximation, local search). The three added units have no source cells (they are gap-fills from CLRS and other recalled benchmarks, marked as such) and every figure in them was measured by `verify/v_f8.py`.
14. **Software engineering, recorded (2026-11-06).** `software-engineering.txt` is two outlines, merged into D22. Their week-by-week order is kept inside D22 but several topics were merged because the outlines overlap: life-cycle models (ISE W2, SEM W2 and W3), requirements (ISE W5, SEM W4), design basics (ISE W7, SEM W5), object-oriented analysis and design (ISE W9, SEM W7 to W9) and testing (ISE W10 and W11, SEM W10 to W12) each form one set of units. Numbers in D22 (COCOMO constants, the Halstead counts, the reliability fits) are recomputed by `verify/v_g1.py` to `v_g3.py`; the textbook constants and the standards are recalled and marked so. Say if you want the Shooman reliability unit (U22.14) removed, since no week of the outline calls for it.
15. **Go on demand, recorded (2026-11-06).** On the user's instruction Go is taught on demand for system design, database-related coding and cloud computing, and Python for everything else. D23 holds the language (U23.1 bridge, interfaces and generics, concurrency, networked services, database coding, system-design building blocks, cloud-native Go, testing and profiling). Limits to know: the build machine could not download modules, so the programs use only the standard library and the SQLite, gRPC and Kubernetes client libraries are named and not used; no container daemon was available, so the Dockerfile and the image size are untested (the static binary and its signal handling were run); the benchmark times are from one machine and are marked as such. Say if any Go-track exercise should stay in Python.
16. **Overlapping and related concepts unified and de-duplicated, recorded (2026-11-06).** On the user's instruction every concept that two or more units taught or built is now taught and built once, by one owner, and the other units keep only what their domain adds and point to the owner (Appendix G lists each concept, its owner and the units that reuse it). The pass found, among others, probability basics taught three times (now U21.6), the Bloom filter and universal hashing built three times (U3.1 and U17.5), consistent hashing in five places (U9.5), shortest paths and spanning trees in the routing bridge and in D17 (D17), the flow and matching build (U17.14), the page-table and TLB build (U4.1), the lock manager, recovery log and precedence graph in the distributed-systems bridge and in D15 (D15), the relational engine in the storage bridge, D15 and the capstone (D15 and U13.8), UML notation (U22.9), and the birthday simulator (U5.1). Coverage of every source cell was re-run after each change.
Resolved on 2026-11-04 and no longer open: the placement of the architecture courses (D14, printed before the capstones), the scope of the GPU labs (three tiers with a simulator fallback) and the assembly language (an AArch64 subset with a crosswalk to the MIPS-like and RISC-V-like forms).

**Everything else** that is a recalled reference, a benchmark title or a standard result is marked *recalled, not checked* where it appears. Everything listed as an Apple-silicon fact for the Mac labs of D14 (commands such as `sysctl hw.cachelinesize`, the 16 KB page size, MLX, the Metal vocabulary, `NUMBA_ENABLE_CUDASIM=1`) is recalled, not checked, and each lab begins by having you verify it on your Mac. Prices in U10.7 are illustrative numbers for an exercise, not current Google Cloud prices. Product names and limits change often: verify them in the console or the documentation before relying on them.

**Safety notes.** Nothing in this document asks you to scan, probe, attack or access a system you do not own. The ethical-hacking and security units use an isolated host-only lab, standard tools and Python models of the mechanisms; no exploit or malware is authored. The hardware-security work in U14.22 is a defensive model in simulation only, and free-GPU labs use a personal account with no secrets in the notebook. Cryptographic code built here is for learning and is never deployed. No assignment asks for credentials, keys or personal data; use synthetic data throughout.
